items.item: Why a cell's own sequence number, not any other cell's state, is the only thing a dequeue call ever consults — which is exactly why a later, published slot cannot rescue a consumer stuck on an earlier, unpublished one

at.step: Empty, not the message, not a wait

items.item: Why 'no lock' and 'lock-free' are different promises: Vyukov's queue has no mutex anywhere in it and is still blocking by the strict definition, because a single suspended producer can hold up a specific consumer forever

Why the recorded stalled-producer history has no legal sequential order at all, while the overlapping version of the same two operations does — the difference is exactly the real-time precedence the linearizability definition tests for, not a property of the queue's implementation

at.step: Checked against the definition, not just read off the code

items.item: Why the Disruptor's own division of labor (Sequence, Sequencer, Sequence Barrier) does not remove the stall risk, only relocates which structure's documentation has to say so — the guide's own warning about an unpublished slot stalling consumers is the same failure Vyukov's queue has, independently derived

items.item: Why padding fixes false sharing without changing what either thread computes: the cost being removed is purely about which cache line each counter's writes invalidate, never about the counters' own values

Why this topic's own measured queue-throughput table (Vyukov's queue losing ground to a mutex as thread count rises on this specific machine) is not evidence that lock-free designs are slower in general — it is one honest result from one oversubscribed, four-core cloud sandbox, with a plausible mechanism (busy-spin vs. a backing-off mutex) named rather than asserted

Why the sequence comparison's three outcomes (equal, less, greater) are jointly exhaustive and mutually exclusive for both enqueue and dequeue — there is no fourth case the algorithm has to handle separately

That the same per-slot lap-counter idea appears in two independently designed systems (Vyukov's sequence number, the Disruptor's per-slot availability tracking) solving the identical coordination problem in a different place in the design, not by coincidence but because any bounded ring shared by many writers needs some per-slot way to say whose turn it is

Why Michael-Scott queues (unbounded, linked, lock-free with helping) are a genuinely different design point than this topic's bounded, array-based, blocking one, not a strictly better alternative — the two solve for different constraints (fixed memory and backpressure vs. unbounded growth)

Why this topic's examples.c is the right place for every throughput and false-sharing number, and examples.py is the right place for every exact, asserted trace and linearizability verdict — conflating the two would either make an unverifiable timing claim look asserted, or make a deterministic logical claim look like it depended on a specific machine
